Today's big story: Anthropic Below Its IPO Price: Do Giants Come Back?

Dell Technologies stock fell 11.8% on Tuesday, Nov 24, to close at $295.28. The S&P 500 slipped 0.5% the same session.

The fall was not a reaction to Dell's results. The company reported after the closing bell that day. The stock fell with most of its group, but further. Ten of the eleven other technology hardware companies worth $2 billion or more ended lower.

Did Dell's Results Cause The Fall?

No. Dell released results for its fiscal third quarter, the three months to October 2026, after Tuesday's close. Revenue was a record $54.9 billion, up 103% from a year earlier. Analysts had expected about $49.3 billion.

Adjusted earnings per share were $9.45. That figure leaves out some costs. Analysts had expected $6.62, so both revenue and adjusted earnings beat estimates.

Dell rose 20.5% on Monday, then fell 11.8% on Tuesday. Swings that size are hard to sit through when one stock holds a big part of the savings you live on. The Trefis Income Solution pays a dividend yield about 3 times the S&P 500's, from 50 companies that have paid dividends for at least 10 years in a row. See what it pays.

Was It Dell Or Its Group?

Dell fell with its group, but much further. Of the 11 other technology hardware companies worth $2 billion or more, 10 fell and 1 rose.

Their median move was a fall of 7.2%, while Dell fell 11.8%. Eight of them fell 5% or more.

Broader measures fell less. XLK, a fund that tracks the technology sector, fell 3.3%. The Nasdaq Composite index fell 1.5%.

On the Trefis peer list for Dell, three companies fell and two rose. HP, Hewlett Packard Enterprise and Cisco Systems fell. International Business Machines and Apple rose. Cisco and IBM are not among the 11 companies counted above.

Hewlett Packard Enterprise fell 16.3%, more than Dell. Before Tuesday's session, it raised its outlook, but its shares fell on worries about its margins.

Where Does Dell Stock Stand Now?

In the year before Tuesday, Dell had one fall at least this large. Counting rises too, it had 8 moves at least this large. The latest was Monday's 20.5% rise.

Over the past year, Dell returned 143.6% including dividends. The S&P 500 returned 10.3% on the same basis. Over the past month, Dell lost 36.8% including dividends.

Its highest close of the past 12 months was $588.40, on Sept 17. Its lowest close of the past 12 months was $111.07, on Jan 20.

The next report covers Dell's fiscal fourth quarter, the three months to January 2027. It is due in February 2027. That report will show how much of Dell's backlog of AI server orders not yet shipped remains. Dell ended its third quarter with a record $132.3 billion of them.

Huang Is Back as NVDA CEO: Quantum ETFs to Buy Before the Next AI Surge
Aparajita Dutta

The technology sector and broader stock market endured a brutal week of turmoil after Nvidia NVDA CEO Jensen Huang abruptly resigned on Nov. 12 amid personal conduct concerns. The incident sent Wall Street tumbling and raised concerns about the outlook for an AI-driven economy. The Nasdaq shed roughly 10% for the week, its worst performance since March 2020, as investors fled high-growth technology names. 

Then came the stunning reversal this Monday, when Nvidia's board unanimously reinstated Huang as president, CEO, and board member, citing input from senior U.S. government officials who concluded his return posed no national security risk. Consequently, Nvidia shares rocketed approximately 32% at the close of Nov. 23 trading session, sending a ripple effect across the advanced-computing complex — and sparking a sharp, double-digit rally in high-beta quantum stocks.

Notably, Rigetti Computing jumped 13%, D-Wave Quantum rallied 12%, IonQ climbed 12.6%, and Quantinuum gained 8.2% at Monday's close, as traders treated Huang's comeback as a sector-wide green light for the AI and quantum trade. 

With sentiment whipsawing from panic to euphoria in just a matter of days, investor spotlight now falls squarely on quantum exchange-traded funds (ETFs), which offer exposure to the sector's rebound while spreading risk across multiple stocks.

But before identifying specific funds, one must understand the deep connections between quantum computing companies and Nvidia — and why Huang's return became such a pivotal moment for the entire sector.

The Nvidia-Quantum Nexus: Why Huang's Comeback Matters

The relationship between Nvidia and quantum computing is not merely thematic; it is technical and increasingly commercial. 

Nvidia develops CUDA-Q, a software platform that bridges classical GPU computing with quantum processors, and the company has been aggressively expanding its quantum ecosystem. In mid-November, Nvidia announced a collaboration with IBM and Fermilab to develop a quantum-classical codesign platform, alongside a breakthrough error-correction algorithm that boasts the capability to accelerate quantum research by up to 13,000x. 

Against this backdrop, in connection with Nvidia's acceleration in quantum computing, many relevant quantum companies have been directly collaborating with the GPU-maker or are indirectly benefiting. 

For instance, IonQ IONQ is currently partnering with NVIDIA to integrate its Superion 256 quantum processing unit (QPU) directly with NVIDIA's AI and supercomputing infrastructure, with on-premise installation scheduled for 2027 at the NVIDIA Accelerated Quantum Research Center ("NVAQC"). The companies had previously collaborated on hybrid research — including work with Oak Ridge National Laboratory and the University of Tennessee on CUDA-Q combinatorial optimization, as well as drug-design research alongside AWS and AstraZeneca.

title: IBM and Microsoft expand Azure Compute Fleet integration
detail:
IBM and Microsoft expand Azure Compute Fleet integration
The integration also allows organisations to use discounted Azure Spot VMs for fault-tolerant workloads. Credit: Erman Gunes / Shutterstock.com · Verdict · Erman Gunes / Shutterstock.com
Shubhendu Vimal

Trading disclosure

IBM and Microsoft have expanded their collaboration with the general availability of IBM Spectrum LSF and IBM Spectrum Collective provider plug-ins for Microsoft Azure Compute Fleet.

The plug-ins connect IBM's workload orchestration software with Azure Compute Fleet for compute-intensive workloads across hybrid environments.

The integration is aimed at applications including electronic design automation, computer-aided engineering, genome sequencing, molecular dynamics, AI training, fine-tuning, data analytics and AI inference.

IBM Spectrum LSF and IBM Spectrum Collective distribute, deploy, orchestrate and optimise workloads across available computing resources.

With the Azure Compute Fleet integration, organisations can provision and release Azure virtual machines (VMs) automatically in response to workload requirements.

Users can specify several eligible Azure VM families and sizes through a single compute fleet request, including HDv2 and HXv2 instances.

This approach is intended to reduce dependence on one VM configuration and improve capacity availability during periods of high demand.

The integration also allows organisations to use discounted Azure Spot VMs for fault-tolerant workloads that can be restarted, while using pay-as-you-go capacity for workloads requiring more continuity.

Companies can add Azure capacity to process queued workloads during peak demand, then release those resources as demand declines.

IBM said the plug-ins enable existing on-premises IBM Spectrum LSF and Spectrum Collective installations to extend into Azure without altering existing job-submission workflows or application scheduling practices.

The companies developed the native integration together to support workload orchestration across on-premises infrastructure, hyperscale cloud platforms and neocloud environments.

Separately, Reuters reported that Microsoft has declared a "Code Red" drive to overhaul how it prevents and responds to major service failures after a 24-hour outage exposed shortcomings in its engineering systems and crisis response, citing internal memos.

The outage on 12-13 November affected governments from Australia and Japan to the US, delayed trading firms and disrupted airline communications.

Microsoft said the incident was not related to cyber activity or AI agents.

Microsoft attributed the outage to an undetected Windows scalability defect introduced in July.

Chief executive Satya Nadella publicly apologised for the disruption.

"IBM and Microsoft expand Azure Compute Fleet integration" was originally created and published by Verdict, a GlobalData owned brand.

Image from Pixabay

Today's big story: Anthropic Below Its IPO Price: Do Giants Come Back?

You may hold International Business Machines (IBM) next to an S&P 500 index fund. Its mainframe, management says, runs 70% of the industry's transaction volume by value. A business that central can make IBM look like the calm part of your money. Every stock adds its own swings to the market's, and wider swings should earn you more. So, measured against the index, has IBM's return over the years made up for how much its shares jump around?

IBM's Swings Have Paid Slightly Better Than The Index's

IBM returned 19.0% a year with dividends from November 16, 2021, to November 24, 2026. That beat the S&P 500's 10.4%, but you took a bumpier ride for it. IBM's annual volatility, how far its price usually strays over a year, was 30.5%, against 17.4% for the index. Divide the return by the volatility and IBM earned 0.623 for each unit of swing. The index earned 0.598. So each bump in IBM's price has paid you a little more than the market's did, but only a little.

IBM's price has swung 30.5% a year, against 17.4% for the S&P 500. That means sitting through deeper drops in the money you keep in it. The Trefis Income Solution owns 50 companies that have each paid dividends for at least 10 years in a row, and together they yield about 3 times what the S&P 500 pays. See the Income Solution.

IBM On The S&P 500's Up And Down Days

In the past year, IBM lost more on the market's bad days than it gained on its good ones. From November 21, 2025, to November 24, 2026, a $10,000 holding in IBM gained $62.40 on an average day the S&P 500 rose. The same sum in the index gained $69.80. On an average down day, the IBM holding lost $74.30, against $65.30 in the index. That is an average, not a rule. On November 5, 2026, the index's worst day of the past year, the S&P 500 fell 4.4% and IBM fell 2.8%.

IBM's own swings were far wider than the market's. Its volatility over the past year was 48.5%, against 15.0% for the index. Yet for each 1% the S&P 500 moved, IBM moved only about 0.77% on average. Its daily moves tracked the index only loosely. Their correlation was 0.24, on a scale where 1 means moving in step. So IBM does not simply magnify the market for you. It adds big swings of its own.

What IBM's Business Says About The Swings Ahead

IBM has a steady core with a lumpy edge. That edge can swing software growth from one quarter to the next. The steady part is software that clients pay for every year. On the October 21, 2026, call, management said this annual recurring revenue grew 8% to $24.9 billion. For all of 2026, IBM expects revenue growth of 4% to 5% at constant currency.

title: What IBM Holders Got Wrong Before The Slide

What IBM Holders Got Wrong Before The Slide
Al Bentley
Tue, November 24, 2026 at 3:10 PM CST 4 min read

Trade IBM on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

If you had been weighing International Business Machines against flashier AI stocks and decided to sit it out, the result may look surprising. Investors who held International Business Machines over the past year are down 21.3%, including dividends. That drop now sits next to earlier research arguing for premium pricing based on hybrid cloud, GenAI and quantum potential. If you were back on 23 November 2025, which assumption or risk on record would you interrogate first?

The move put International Business Machines in the middle of this trade. Scan 53 AI infrastructure stocks for other companies exposed to it.

The Two IBM Stories Investors Had To Weigh

The shares cost US$297 at the start of the period, and investors in International Business Machines were choosing between two sharply different stories about what that price implied.

The bullish narrative saw a Fair Value of US$350, effectively a price that assumed hybrid cloud, GenAI and quantum efforts would support stronger long term software margins, with profit margin assumptions rising from 9.1% to 15.9% by 2028.

The more cautious view anchored on a Fair Value of US$282, built on the idea that hybrid cloud and AI could lift results, but that macro uncertainty and competition might hold profit margins closer to 14.1% by 2028.

NYSE:IBM 1-Year Stock Price Chart
What The IBM Results Actually Tested

The sharp Q2 2026 warning that International Business Machines linked to an AI driven shift toward hardware spending challenged the bullish case that software and hybrid cloud would steadily lift margins. Later Q3 2026 figures showed revenue at US$17,103m and net income at US$2,200m, with net margin at 12.9%. The evidence cut both ways.

The real hinge was not excitement about AI, quantum or chips. It was whether IBM could keep net margin moving toward the thesis. For any other stock built on a margin story, it can be useful to track the gap between the forecast margin path and the figure printed in each quarterly report.

What IBM's Lower Price Now Asks You To Believe

International Business Machines trades at US$233 today, and the bullish analyst Narrative on Simply Wall St places its Fair Value above that level based on a richer mix of recurring software, hybrid cloud and AI focused consulting.

The fall over the past year only looks like a potential opening if a buyer believes recurring software, AI heavy consulting and distributed infrastructure can collectively outweigh mainframe swings and CapEx sensitive contracts.

"The current valuation implies the market is pricing IBM's shares as if the Q2 2026 revenue shortfall, guidance reduction to 4–5% growth and mainframe volatility will weigh more heavily on long term cash generation than the growth in recurring software ARR, hybrid cloud, AI consulting and quantum investments."

What Would A Short Seller Say About IBM Stock?
Trefis Team

Today's big story: Nvidia Added $954 Billion In A Day. Is Jensen Huang Too Big To Fire?

International Business Machines (IBM) stock returned -17.6%, dividends included, in the year to Monday, November 23. The S&P 500 returned 12%. Yet the business grew. Revenue rose 6.8% in the four quarters to September 2026. The operating margin, the share of sales left after running costs, rose to 18.3% from 17.7% a year earlier.

Management did not blame an outside cause. On its October 21 call, it spoke of "strength across our portfolio and solid execution". A short seller, someone who bets a stock will keep falling, would still push on three points. Rivals grow faster, IBM's growth has been uneven, and its debt is heavier than the market's.

Are IBM's rivals growing faster?

Yes, three of the four peers we compare grew faster. Alphabet grew revenue 22.2% and Microsoft grew 17.9%. Amazon.com grew 15.4%. Only Accenture grew about as slowly as IBM, at 6.5%. Each company is measured over its own latest four quarters.

IBM stock lost 17.6% in a year, dividends included, even as its revenue grew 6.8%. If IBM is a large part of your savings and you live on its dividend, that is a long fall to sit through. The Trefis Income Solution pays a dividend yield about 3 times the S&P 500's, from 50 companies that have paid dividends for at least 10 years in a row. See what it pays.

Slow sales growth is not a long-running problem at IBM. Yearly growth rose from 1.1% in the four quarters to September 2023 to 6.8% now. The quarters were uneven, though. Revenue grew 12.2% in the quarter to December 2025 and 9.5% in the quarter to March 2026. It then grew 1.1% in the quarter to June and 4.7% in the quarter to September.

What did IBM's managers say about the uneven quarters?

Management named its own cause for the soft June quarter. "Last quarter, it impacted our software growth by 4-5 points when we were down double-digit transactional," a manager said.

Transaction processing (TP) software then grew 10% in the September quarter. "I do not expect double-digit performance in TP to keep going," a manager said candidly. Management also said about a quarter of the software speed-up came from deals that slipped from earlier quarters. So part of the September bounce was timing.

Does the cash show strain for an owner?

The payout does not. Free cash flow, the cash left after running the business and buying equipment, was $14 billion over four quarters. Dividends took $6.3 billion and buybacks about $1 billion.

Debt is the softer spot. It stood at $67.1 billion, up from $59 billion five years earlier. That equals 30.5% of IBM's market value, against 20.2% for the S&P 500.

Buy-and-hold dividend growth investors know something about the best dividend stocks to buy that less experienced yield-hunters don't: it pays to be patient when you're investing for income.

Shares in companies that raise their payouts like clockwork decade after decade can produce superior total returns (price change plus dividends) over the long run, even if they sport apparently ho-hum yields to begin with.

That's partly because regular dividend increases lift the yield on an investor's original cost basis. Stick around long enough, and the modest yield you received on your initial investment can hit double digits one day.

Companies with long histories of annual dividend growth also offer some peace of mind. After all, any company that manages to raise its dividend year after year — through recession, war, market crashes and more — is demonstrating both its financial resilience and its commitment to returning cash to shareholders.

What can dividend growth stocks do for long-term returns?

"The S&P 500 Dividend Aristocrats exhibits both capital growth and dividend income characteristics," writes Rupert Watts, head of factors and dividends at S&P Dow Jones Indices. "Over the long term, the S&P 500 Dividend Aristocrats exhibited higher returns with lower volatility compared with the S&P 500, resulting in higher risk-adjusted returns."

Put another way, dividend growers not only go along for the ride in bull markets, but they also tend to hold up better in market drawdowns.

Case in point: The S&P 500 Dividend Aristocrats Index lost 6.2% on a total return basis in 2022 — better than the S&P 500's 18.1% decline.

And dividends are an important element of overall returns, say Argus Research Director of Portfolio Strategies John Eade and Director of Research Jim Kelleher.

Citing data from Ned Davis Research, the two note that the average annual return of stocks within the S&P 500 between 1972 and 2010 was 7.3%, but the average annual return for companies that initiated or raised their dividends was 9.6%.

"Stable and increasing dividends also act as a signal of management's confidence in their firm's prospects," Watts adds. Additionally, investors consider such track records as a sign of corporate maturity and balance sheet strength.

How do you find the best dividend stocks to buy?
Credit: Getty Images

If you're looking to add dependable dividend growers to your portfolio, you can start by checking out the S&P 500 Dividend Aristocrats, an index of 69 companies in the S&P 500 that have raised their payouts annually for at least 25 consecutive years.
